claims.text: The material family under consideration is fcc Fe-Co-Ni-based high-entropy alloys, including equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The targeted property is the stacking fault energy.
Standard static DFT significantly underestimates the magnetic orbital-moment contribution to stacking fault energy.
The alleged underestimation of the orbital-moment contribution is caused by neglecting longitudinal spin fluctuations.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations induce sizable thermal magnetic moments in Co, Cr, and Ni.
Co, Cr, and Ni have zero or negligible moments in the corresponding static calculations.
The relevant state is paramagnetic CoCrFeMnNi in fcc and hcp structures over 50–1200 K.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations alter magneto-volume coupling and the magnetic-entropy contribution to stacking fault energy.
LSFs can be incorporated through a DLM treatment combined with CPA and a fluctuating-medium approximation.
The calculations model temperature-dependent magnetic behavior from 50 to 1200 K and vary Wigner-Seitz radii to represent lattice expansion.
The calculations compare fcc and hcp structures under ambient pressure.
LSF-induced moments modify both magnetic entropy and internal-energy contributions to free energy.
Stacking fault energy increases monotonically with temperature because of magneto-volume coupling.
The calculated stacking fault energy changes from negative at cryogenic temperatures to positive at elevated temperatures.
The temperature-dependent stacking fault energy shifts the energetic balance between fcc and hcp phases.
Positive stacking fault energy at higher temperatures promotes nano-twin formation.
The LSF calculation agrees better with experimental phase stability and defect formation than floating-spin calculations.
Explicit phonon effects are omitted and may explain a predicted fcc–hcp transition temperature near 430 K rather than the experimental value near 633 K.
Structural relaxation of faulted supercells was omitted and may affect the magnitude of the interfacial energy.
Failure of the LSF model to reproduce the measured sign or temperature trend of stacking fault energy would falsify the proposed mechanism.
